defs: Ensuring information is protected from unauthorized access or disclosure.

Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability—the three foundational objectives of information security.

course.learn: The CIA Triad organizes security goals into confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Confidentiality limits unauthorized disclosure, integrity protects accuracy and trustworthiness, and availability keeps systems and data accessible to authorized users when needed.
course.why: Most security controls protect one or more of these three objectives, so the triad gives you a quick way to classify what a scenario is trying to protect.
course.example: Full-disk encryption protects data on a stolen laptop; hashing can detect unauthorized file changes; redundant servers help maintain availability.
course.exam: CompTIA often asks which CIA component is MOST directly affected. Ask: was data exposed, changed, or made unavailable?

breakdown.explanation: Protects information from unauthorized access or disclosure. Common protections include encryption, access controls, and authentication.
Ensures data remains accurate, complete, and unaltered without authorization. Hashing, digital signatures, and permissions can help protect integrity.
Ensures authorized users can access systems and data when needed. Redundancy, backups, fault tolerance, and disaster recovery help maintain availability.

slides.title: Relationship Between the CIA Components
slides.raw:
Relationship Between
the CIA Components
• Confidentiality and integrity
• Integrity and availability
• Confidentiality and availability
slides.teach: Know what each component does and how the components work together. CompTIA often asks which component best fits a scenario.
defs: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability—the three foundational information-security objectives.

course.learn: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability overlap. A single control can protect multiple CIA objectives, and improving one objective can sometimes create tradeoffs with another.
course.why: Security design usually requires balancing all three CIA objectives. Strengthening one objective should not unnecessarily weaken another.
course.example: Encrypting a database protects confidentiality, but if the encryption keys are lost or unavailable, authorized users may no longer be able to access the data, creating an availability problem.
course.exam: When several CIA components seem affected, choose the one MOST directly described by the scenario.

breakdown.explanation: Controls that restrict unauthorized access can also help prevent unauthorized changes. For example, access controls can protect both who can view data and who can modify it.
Information must be both accurate and accessible to be useful. Backups, redundancy, and integrity checks can help ensure reliable data remains available after a failure or attack.
Security must protect information from unauthorized access while keeping it accessible to authorized users. Controls that are too restrictive can improve confidentiality but reduce availability.

course.learn: A confidentiality compromise happens when information is disclosed to someone who is not authorized to see it. The cause can be technical, physical, or human.
course.why: Sensitive information loses value and can create legal, financial, or safety consequences once unauthorized parties gain access.
course.example: An employee emails a confidential report to the wrong external address, or an attacker steals unencrypted customer records.
course.exam: Exposure, disclosure, eavesdropping, data leakage, and unauthorized viewing point toward confidentiality.

breakdown.explanation: Accidental actions can expose sensitive information, such as sending data to the wrong recipient, sharing credentials, or misconfiguring permissions.
Software bugs, system failures, or incorrect technical configurations can expose information that should remain private.
Attackers manipulate people into revealing sensitive information, granting access, or bypassing security procedures by exploiting trust, urgency, fear, or authority.
Authorized users can intentionally steal, disclose, or misuse sensitive information because their legitimate access gives them a path to the data.
Theft, tailgating, unauthorized facility access, or exposed documents and devices can allow sensitive information to be viewed or removed.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Protecting confidentiality means controlling who can view information and preventing unauthorized disclosure. Common layers include physical security, authentication, authorization, encryption, training, and monitoring.
course.why: No single control protects every path to sensitive data, so confidentiality normally requires defense in depth.
course.example: A company encrypts laptops, requires MFA, limits file permissions, and monitors unusual downloads.
course.exam: When the goal is secrecy, favor access control and encryption over availability controls such as clustering.

breakdown.explanation: Physical security limits unauthorized access to buildings, devices, documents, and other locations where sensitive information is stored or processed.
Authentication verifies identity, while access controls and authorization determine which resources an authenticated user is allowed to view or use.
Training teaches users how to recognize phishing, protect credentials, handle sensitive information, and follow procedures that reduce accidental disclosure.
Monitoring and auditing track access and activity so organizations can identify unusual behavior, policy violations, and possible unauthorized disclosure.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Methods to Protect Confidentiality and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Protecting confidentiality means controlling who can view information and preventing unauthorized disclosure. Common layers include physical security, authentication, authorization, encryption, training, and monitoring. Key ideas include: Physical security; Access control & authentication; Security awareness & training; Monitoring & auditing.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.learn: An integrity compromise means data, software, or configuration has been changed in an unauthorized or untrustworthy way. Changes may be malicious or accidental.
course.why: Organizations make decisions based on data. If the data cannot be trusted, the system can produce harmful or incorrect results.
course.example: An attacker modifies payroll records, or a corrupted update changes application files unexpectedly.
course.exam: Unauthorized modification, tampering, corruption, and incorrect data point toward integrity.

breakdown.explanation: Mistakes such as incorrect data entry, accidental deletion, or unintended configuration changes can make information incomplete, inaccurate, or unreliable.
Attackers or insiders may intentionally alter files, records, software, or configurations to manipulate information or disrupt trusted operations.
Weak change controls, poor permissions, software defects, or insecure processes can allow incorrect or unauthorized changes to spread through a system.
Power loss, overheating, water damage, storage failures, and other environmental problems can corrupt data or damage systems that store and process it.

defs.definition: Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.learn: Integrity controls help prove that information is complete, accurate, and unchanged except by authorized processes. Hashing, digital signatures, permissions, change control, and file-integrity monitoring are common examples.
course.why: Integrity lets users trust that the information or software they receive is the same information that was intended.
course.example: A software publisher signs an update, and the client verifies the signature before installing it.
course.exam: Hashing and digital signatures are strong integrity clues. Remember that a digital signature also supports authentication and non-repudiation.

breakdown.explanation: Secure configurations, patching, least privilege, hashing, digital signatures, and file-integrity monitoring help prevent or detect unauthorized changes.
Training users to follow approved change procedures, verify information, protect credentials, and report suspicious activity helps prevent accidental and unauthorized modifications.
Locks, access controls, surveillance, and secure storage protect devices and media from theft, tampering, or unauthorized physical changes.
Regular audits, reviews, testing, patching, and lessons learned help organizations find weaknesses and improve integrity controls over time.

defs.definition: Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Methods to Protect Integrity and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Integrity controls help prove that information is complete, accurate, and unchanged except by authorized processes. Hashing, digital signatures, permissions, change control, and file-integrity monitoring are common examples. Key ideas include: Strengthening your system; Empowering your users; Physical security measures; Continuous improvement.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.

course.learn: An availability compromise prevents authorized users from accessing a system, service, or data when they need it. Outages can be caused by attacks, failures, disasters, or mistakes.
course.why: Security is not useful if legitimate users cannot perform required work. Availability is especially important for critical services.
course.example: A DDoS attack overwhelms a web service, or a failed power supply takes down a server with no redundancy.
course.exam: Outage, downtime, denial of service, failed hardware, and inaccessible resources point toward availability.

breakdown.explanation: Hardware failures, software crashes, network problems, and capacity issues can interrupt services and prevent authorized users from accessing resources.
DDoS attacks, ransomware, malware, and resource-exhaustion attacks can intentionally make systems, services, or data unavailable.
Power outages, natural disasters, internet service failures, fires, floods, and other events outside the organization can cause downtime.
Accidental deletion, incorrect configuration changes, failed maintenance, or unplugging critical equipment can disrupt otherwise healthy systems.

defs.definition: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.

defs: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.

course.learn: Availability is protected through redundancy, maintenance, monitoring, backups, disaster recovery, failover, resilient power, and capacity planning.
course.why: Resilient design removes single points of failure and reduces recovery time after disruption.
course.example: Two web servers sit behind a load balancer so traffic can continue if one server fails.
course.exam: Look for uptime, redundancy, failover, backups, alternate sites, UPS, generators, clustering, and load balancing.

breakdown.explanation: Redundant systems, backups, alternate sites, and recovery plans provide replacement resources and restore operations after a failure or disaster.
Regular patching, monitoring, capacity planning, hardware maintenance, and testing help identify problems before they cause outages.
Firewalls, DDoS protections, segmentation, endpoint security, and monitoring help prevent attacks from interrupting critical services.
Training, documented procedures, change management, and clear responsibilities reduce outages caused by mistakes or improper system changes.

defs.definition: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
